content: The presence of non-medical staff and peer counselors was highly valued by clients. Médicos del Mundo (MdM) is an independent humanitarian organization that provides both emergency and long-term psychosocial support, as well as clinical care, to vulnerable populations. Since 2003, MdM has been conducting traditional HIV testing, and since 2007, it has been offering rapid diagnostic testing. These services are available at branch locations in various cities across Spain. HIV testing services (HTS) are primarily targeted at socially excluded individuals at high risk of HIV infection, including sex workers, drug users, and undocumented migrants. MdM emphasizes the use of services provided through the National Health System (NHS) to deliver information and HTS. For those hesitant to use public healthcare, MdM either accompanies them to NHS services or offers testing within MdM branch offices. Free rapid HIV tests using fingerstick whole blood or oral fluid are conducted alongside preand post-test counseling. All services at MdM branches are delivered by a multidisciplinary team, including supervised lay providers trained according to WHO guidelines. Individuals with reactive HIV test results are referred to public hospital HIV/AIDS units for confirmatory testing. Those diagnosed as HIV-positive are linked to treatment and care. For undocumented migrants, MdM provides guidance and support to help them access benefits from the NHS. Confidentiality of tests and results is strictly maintained, adhering to Spain’s data protection laws. Between 2008 and 2012, 3,251 individuals were tested and referred to public hospitals for confirmatory HIV testing. Among them, 2,253 were women, 897 were men, and 101 were transgender individuals. The program identified 72 new HIV diagnoses confirmed by public hospitals. A key factor in the program’s success is the provision of free, walk-in services without requiring personal identification. These services complement traditional HIV testing programs offered through the NHS. In India, HIV testing facilities screen clients for symptoms suggestive of pulmonary or extrapulmonary tuberculosis (TB) as part of pre-test counseling. Symptomatic patients are systematically referred for further investigations at the same facility. This activity is routinely reported at district, state, and national levels. Since 2005, Médecins du Monde (MdM) has implemented a harm reduction program in Yangon, Myanmar, targeting populations at high risk of unsafe sexual practices, including female sex workers, men who have sex with men (MSM), and transgender individuals. The program, developed in collaboration with affected populations, offers a comprehensive range of services through outreach and drop-in centers. These services include health education, behavior change communication, condom promotion and distribution, HTS, STI testing and treatment, HIV care (including treatment for opportunistic infections and antiretroviral therapy), and psychosocial support. Peer-led outreach enables the program to reach high-risk populations in settings such as brothels, karaoke bars, and nightclubs. Clients visiting drop-in centers can access medical care, participate in recreational and social activities, or simply relax. Additional activities include health-oriented entertainment events, meditation, games, hairdressing, and manicures. A tea shop near the drop-in center, managed by an HIV/AIDS self-support group, provides low-cost drinks and salads, while free lunches are offered to clients attending the clinic or waiting for HIV test results. All services are delivered in a user-friendly, non-discriminatory, and sensitive environment. In 2014, 668 female sex workers and 637 MSM accessed HTS at the Yangon drop-in center. Among them, 130 female sex workers (19%) and 190 MSM (30%) tested HIV-positive and received a second rapid test on-site. Eight percent had inconclusive results and were asked to return in six weeks for repeat testing. Newly diagnosed HIV-positive clients were referred for antiretroviral therapy (ART). By the end of 2014, 32% of newly tested female sex workers and 33% of newly tested MSM were on ART. Retention rates on ART have historically been high, with 24-month retention rates of 85% for female sex workers and 90% for MSM. Over 99% of clients accessing testing at MdM since the program’s inception have received their test results, with more than 84% of female sex workers and 90% of MSM knowing their status. However, many sex workers face barriers to accessing fixed-location facilities due to distance, time constraints, and travel restrictions imposed by their pimps. In Hong Kong, HTS provided by AIDS Concern primarily targets MSM, clients of female sex workers, and youth at high risk of HIV infection. Services are offered in collaboration with gay bar owners, escort services, and youth centers, which provide venues for testing. Mobile outreach extends services to remote areas. The Government Department of Health provides technical support. To increase awareness and uptake of HTS, AIDS Concern uses social media, online appointment scheduling, and multimedia campaigns. Anonymous surveys conducted during HTS collect data on client characteristics, testing behavior, and condom use, enabling service improvement and adaptation. In 2014, AIDS Concern conducted over 4,000 rapid HIV tests, identifying 53 positive cases among 2,258 tests conducted for MSM. The program’s success is attributed to strong community engagement and additional training for HTS workers to enhance capacity and sensitivity. Despite success, barriers such as stigma and low risk perception among young MSM persist. In Cambodia, the 2008 law on human trafficking and sexual exploitation criminalized prostitution, leading many women to work in non-brothel-based entertainment establishments. Cambodian Women for Peace and Development (CWPD) implemented HTS in urban areas within entertainment establishments or through freelance services in homes and counseling centers. Peer providers, selected from entertainment workers, are trained to offer HTS. In 2014, 52% of entertainment service workers at the CWPD Battambang site received HIV testing. Eight workers had reactive test results, seven of whom were confirmed HIV-positive and linked to treatment and care. Clients testing HIV-negative received post-test counseling and risk reduction messages. In Chengdu, China, the “1+N” community-based HTS program focuses on MSM. Collaboration with local Centers for Disease Control (CDC) ensures high-quality HTS, including rapid HIV testing, preand post-test counseling, confirmatory testing, and referrals for HIV-positive individuals. Mobile HTS is offered in gay saunas and near escort services. Peer volunteers are trained to provide anonymous rapid HIV testing, reducing stigma and discrimination. Recruitment methods include outreach at gay venues, online recruitment, and word-of-mouth. By 2014, the program had provided HTS to 18,683 MSM, diagnosing approximately 250 HIV-positive cases annually and retaining 85% in care for over a year. In Cebu City, Philippines, Transgender COLORS Inc. works to promote equality and health for transgender individuals. The Feminina Trans program, implemented by COLORS, educates and reduces stigma toward transgender people and HIV health issues while enhancing access to HIV prevention, treatment, and care. HTS is provided by peer educators through group lectures and one-on-one sessions. In 2014, 508 transgender women were reached, with 7% diagnosed HIV-positive and referred for treatment. Client satisfaction surveys showed 99% satisfaction with services, highlighting the supportive and comfortable environment provided by peer educators and staff. In Guangzhou, China, the Lingnan Partners Community Support Center (LPCSC) provides HTS primarily to MSM and transgender individuals. Since 2008, with support from the Guangzhou CDC, HTS has expanded to eight locations across five cities. LPCSC also offers online HIV prevention services, including risk self-assessment, a 24-hour test scheduler, and anonymous partner notification. Since 2014, HIV self-testing kits have been available, supported by online counseling and referrals for confirmatory testing.
